clue.text: Not large, just ten stone

indicators.note: saying a thing is not present tells you to take its letter away from the word beside it

parts.note: just, in the sense of merely or solely
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Someone is told a gem is small: it weighs a mere ten stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone' reads as a weight, the British unit of fourteen pounds, but here it is the gem.
explanation.definitionFit: Onyx is a banded variety of chalcedony, a semi-precious mineral cut for jewellery and cameos.

clue.text: At home after missing work to accept special kinky deliveries

indicators.note: something that accepts another takes it inside, so one piece receives the other

parts.note: someone missing work is off, as in off sick
SP is an abbreviation for special
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A person skips work to stay in and take delivery of some saucy parcels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the home word behind the absence word, and the pair then take special inside. Off spin is a cricket term for bowling that turns sharply after bouncing.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a delivery is a ball bowled, and off spin deliveries deviate sideways, so bent or twisted balls are fairly called kinky.

clue.text: Regularly missed him on cat, say, at sea?

definitions.text: Regularly missed him on cat, say, at sea?

indicators.note: being at sea is being confused and all over the place, so the letters get jumbled
dropping letters at regular intervals leaves every other one standing

parts.note: the second and fourth letters are skipped, keeping the first, third and fifth
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a man aboard a catamaran, out on the water, was often missed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a cat is a catamaran, so a man on one at sea is a sailor of that kind. 'Cat' wants to be the pet but it is the boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A catamaran is a type of sailing craft, and a man sailing one out on the water is a sailor of such vessels.

clue.text: Environmentalists agree with Pence? Unlikely

indicators.note: an unlikely version is an improbable rearrangement of what came before, so the letters get reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Would green campaigners ever side with Mike Pence, the former US vice-president? Hardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlikely' reads as a comment on the politics but is the signal to rearrange; 'with' only joins the two words of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenpeace is an international campaigning organisation devoted to protecting nature, oceans and climate, so its members are environmentalists.

clue.text: Method often leading to issue for dancer's core strength

definitions.note: names the first word of the phrase 'rhythm method', not a synonym for method
definitions.meaning: a contraceptive technique of timing that is notoriously unreliable, so it often results in children
a dancer's essential gift is a sense of beat

explanation.surface: A training regime for dancers which builds core strength is said to produce a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' reads as a problem, but it is the old word for offspring. The rhythm method avoids pregnancy by timing, and fails often enough to be a standing joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping time to a beat is the most basic talent any dancer needs, and the first word of the contraceptive technique.

clue.text: Sleep, terribly bored by leading barrister's argument

indicators.note: a thing bored by a drill has something driven into its middle
something done terribly is done badly and out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
top, as in the leading position

explanation.surface: A lawyer's case is so dull it sends everyone to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading barrister' looks like a senior counsel, but 'leading' is a separate piece and the definition is only the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Estoppel is a legal principle a lawyer can raise in court, stopping a party from denying something they previously asserted.

clue.text: Remarkably nice rich man in public relations, king when family's gone?

definitions.text: Remarkably nice rich man in public relations, king when family's gone?

indicators.note: something done remarkably is done in an unusual way, so the letters take an unusual order
once a group of relatives has left, those letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written except for the two-letter joining word, which drops out: the fodder is NICE RICH MAN
PR is the standard abbreviation for public relations
taken as written
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: A pleasant wealthy PR man turns out to be royalty once his relatives have departed.
explanation.walkthrough: NICE RICH MAN in PR are shuffled together; KING without KIN leaves G. The whole clue also sketches the fairy-tale hero: a nice rich man who is a royal heir.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy-tale suitor is handsome, wealthy and kind, heir to a throne, which is exactly what the whole clue describes.

clue.text: To the French, taking leave

parts.note: surface: a phrase addressed or dedicated to the people of France
setter's reading: the word French speakers use when saying goodbye, which literally means 'to God'

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a dedication or a toast, but the clue asks what the French say when departing; the French farewell is built from a preposition meaning 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French farewell literally means commending someone to God and is used when parting for a long time.

clue.text: Boffin I don't understand tackles Germans over European bill

indicators.note: in a down entry, being over something means sitting above it, so the first part comes first
to tackle someone is to grab them round the middle, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: eh? is what you say when you don't follow
G is the abbreviation for German, doubled for the plural
E is the abbreviation for European
an ad is a bill or poster

explanation.surface: A scientist admits bafflement while wrestling Germans about a Brussels bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like legislation but is a poster. A boffin is British slang for a scientist or expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a highly intellectual person, especially a clever scientist or academic type.

clue.text: Try to inhibit spread of bacteria in the underground

parts.note: to counter something is to act against it
a culture is a colony of bacteria grown in a dish

explanation.surface: An attempt to stop germs spreading on the London Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The underground' pretends to be the Tube railway; here it is the alternative scene of dissent and rebellion.
explanation.definitionFit: An underground movement is a subculture opposed to mainstream values, especially the hippie-era alternative scene of the 1960s.

clue.text: Where workers make Conservatives rich, before finally getting sacked

indicators.note: the last letter is dismissed from its job, so it is dropped from the end
coming before puts the first piece at the front of the rest

parts.note: fat, as in rich food or a fat cheque
two Conservatives: C, the abbreviation, and TORY, the nickname

explanation.surface: A left-wing jibe: employees toil to enrich the Tories, and then lose their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Conservatives' supplies two pieces, the abbreviation and the nickname. Tory is the everyday name for Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A factory is an industrial building where employees manufacture goods, so it is the place labourers produce things.

clue.text: After covering bathroom wall, one fills

definitions.note: a preposition defining a participle: tailing someone is coming after them

indicators.note: to fill something is to go inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: tiling is the usual finish on a bathroom wall
a means one

explanation.surface: Once the bathroom wall has been tiled, somebody applies filler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' reads as a time word starting the sentence, but it is the definition; A goes inside TILING just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tailing someone means following close behind them, as a detective does, so it loosely corresponds to coming behind.

clue.text: Brief foreign version of Trump: the Movie

parts.note: Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, as a foreign counterpart of the American one
taken as written
a picture is a film

explanation.surface: A short Russian remake of a film about Donald Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' reads as an adjective meaning short, but it is a verb: to brief someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone in the picture is an idiom for informing them fully about a situation, just as a briefing does.

clue.text: Maybe one new waterfront feature in 'ull?

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
the Humber estuary is Hull's waterfront, and the apostrophe shows the local habit of dropping the H

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a new development on the Hull waterfront might be a single item.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a port city in Yorkshire on the Humber estuary; writing it 'ull signals that the H is dropped from the river too.
explanation.definitionFit: One is an example of a numeral, so 'maybe one' defines the answer by giving an instance of it.

clue.text: Dead series of notes for a scraped bass, perhaps

definitions.note: describes the fish rather than naming it: the answer is what a scraped bass is

indicators.note: one thing given for another is swapped in to replace it

parts.note: taken as written
a scale is a sequence of musical notes
taken as written, the letter being swapped out

explanation.surface: A musician's dead scale practice for a double bass that has been scraped.
explanation.walkthrough: SCALE replaces the A of DEAD. 'Bass' and 'notes' push towards music, but the bass is the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A bass is a fish, and scraping one prepares it for cooking by removing the flaky skin covering.

clue.text: Famous Roman fighter preferring death to lions' innards

indicators.note: preferring one thing to another means choosing it instead, so it takes the other's place

parts.note: a legionary was a soldier in a Roman legion
death is one's end
the inside letters of lions

explanation.surface: A gladiator would sooner die than be torn apart by lions in the arena.
explanation.walkthrough: In LEGIONARY the ION is swapped out for END. The arena picture makes 'fighter' look like a gladiator.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone legendary is so renowned that stories are told about them, which makes them extremely well known.

clue.text: Each sporting replay includes period of extra time

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside the other
sporting means playing about, so the letters frolic into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
EA is the abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: Every sports replay features a spell of added time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra time' belongs to football, but here it is the additional day in February.
explanation.definitionFit: A leap year is a calendar year of 366 days, containing one additional day at the end of February.

clue.text: Handle report of Hillary's usurper in the White House

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the answer is how the name sounds when spoken

parts.words: Hillary's usurper in the White House
parts.note: Monica Lewinsky, whose affair with Bill Clinton displaced his wife Hillary

explanation.surface: A news report about the woman who took Hillary Clinton's place in the White House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a verb about dealing with a report, but it is slang for a name; in a non-rhotic British accent the name and the answer sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Handle is informal slang for a person's name or nickname, and so is the answer, also spelt moniker.

clue.text: Stop going north by Cape Wrath

indicators.note: in a down entry, travelling northward means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a dam stops a river
a ness is a headland or cape, as in Loch Ness country place names

explanation.surface: An instruction not to travel north beyond Cape Wrath, the far north-west tip of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Cape Wrath is a real Scottish headland, which welds 'Cape' and 'Wrath' together; split them and 'Wrath' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Madness can mean anger or fury, especially in American usage, so it sits comfortably with rage and ire.

clue.text: What professor did wrong in lecture

indicators.note: a lecture is delivered by voice, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: An academic made a mistake during a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: A tort is a legal wrong, such as negligence; in a British accent it sounds identical to the past tense of teach.
explanation.definitionFit: Professors give lectures and tutorials, so the past tense of instructing students describes their job.

clue.text: Marmoset's tail stretched out like a caterpillar

indicators.note: a tail is the very end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the monkey's name
the rack was a torture device that stretched its victims

explanation.surface: A monkey's tail is extended and looks like a caterpillar.
explanation.walkthrough: The caterpillar is not the insect but the continuous track on a bulldozer or tank, the trade name Caterpillar.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle running on continuous caterpillar treads rather than wheels is described as a tracked vehicle.

clue.text: In verse, Eliot finally admitted to terrible crime

indicators.note: being admitted to a place means being let inside it
something terrible is a mess, so the letters are in disorder

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the last letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of the poet's name

explanation.surface: T. S. Eliot at last confesses, in a poem, to an awful crime.
explanation.walkthrough: CRIME rearranged as MERIC takes T after its second letter. 'In verse' opens the sentence like a scene-setter but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Metric describes poetry written in regular metre, so something metrical is composed in poetic lines with rhythm.

clue.text: Dreadful complaint of two windbags

parts.note: surface: a grumble about a pair of tiresome talkers
setter's reading: the windbags are lungs, and the complaint is an illness affecting both

explanation.walkthrough: 'Windbags' suggests boring people and 'complaint' a grievance; read literally, the bags of wind are the two lungs and the complaint is a disease.
explanation.definitionFit: The illness is a lung infection affecting both lungs at once, a serious and dangerous medical condition.

clue.text: Die-hard Géricault raftsmen swept away fore and aft

indicators.note: with the front and back washed away, only a stretch from the middle of the words remains

parts.note: the end of the painter's name running into the start of the next word

explanation.surface: The stubborn crew on Géricault's raft are washed off at both ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Géricault painted The Raft of the Medusa, showing shipwrecked men on a raft, which fits 'swept away'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is an extremist who holds uncompromising views, just as a die-hard refuses to give up a position.

clue.text: Squeeze into shape once actual start of diet's embraced

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-husband

indicators.note: something embraced is held in the arms, so it ends up inside another piece

parts.note: actual and true both mean real

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of diet

explanation.surface: Someone once tried to squeeze into a figure by actually starting a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeeze into shape' suggests a tight dress, but it is manufacturing; 'once' gives the prefix meaning former.
explanation.definitionFit: Extruding forces soft material such as plastic or metal through a die to form a continuous shaped length.

clue.text: Turn over illegally imported wine

parts.note: to run goods is to smuggle them, as in gun-running
sack is an old word for sherry-type white wine, Falstaff's favourite

explanation.surface: Customs officers are told to hand over wine that was smuggled in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn over' seems to be an instruction to surrender the goods, but it means to search a place roughly.
explanation.definitionFit: Police or burglars turning over a house search it thoroughly and messily, which is exactly what ransacking means.

clue.text: Rascal's hat, say, Derby?

parts.note: taken as written
a cap is a hat
e.g. means for example, like 'say'
the Derby is a famous horse race run at Epsom

explanation.surface: Is the rogue's hat a bowler, which the British call a derby?
explanation.walkthrough: A derby is the American name for a bowler hat, so 'hat' and 'Derby' look like one idea; the Derby is a racing fixture instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A scapegrace is an old-fashioned word for a mischievous scamp or ne'er-do-well, a charming rogue.

clue.text: Old English musician using the bus or car, briefly

indicators.note: briefly means in shortened form, so letters are trimmed from a word

parts.note: travelling by road

explanation.surface: A musician from England's past travels by bus or car.
explanation.walkthrough: Road is shortened to its standard abbreviation RD. William Byrd was a Tudor composer of church music and madrigals, working under Elizabeth I.
explanation.definitionFit: William Byrd was a sixteenth-century composer of choral and keyboard works, one of England's greatest.
